title: ComPhy: Composing Physical Models with end-to-end Alignment
claim: Each equation in a coupled system gets its own learner, and the learners are linked through shared derivatives.
layout: 2 rows, left-to-right, central alignment block with vertical arrows
description: The figure has two horizontal rows, each flowing left to right. Each row starts with a green trapezoid holding an MLP. Row 1's MLP takes inputs x, y and t and outputs û and p̂. Row 2's MLP takes the same inputs and outputs only û. An arrow leads from each MLP into a blue rounded box labeled AD, which holds small boxes of partial derivatives. Row 1 shows derivatives of p and û. Row 2 shows derivatives of û with respect to x, y and t. A black arrow leads from each AD box to an orange box that states a PDE and an initial condition. The top box is labeled PINN and gives the momentum equation. The bottom box is labeled NCL, PINN and gives the divergence-free condition. A red ALIGNMENT box sits between the rows. Red arrows connect it to the shared û-derivative boxes in both AD blocks. The eye goes first to the red box in the middle.
caption: Visual representation of ComPhy for the Navier-Stokes equations. Each module (in this case, PINN or NCL) learns one PDE. The derivatives of each module, computed with Automatic Differentiation (AD) (Baydin et al., 2018), are used to optimize each PDE and to align the other module. CP only uses the first module for inference as it predicts all the variables of the system.
abstract: Real-world phenomena typically involve multiple, interwoven dynamics that can be elegantly captured by systems of Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). However, accurately solving such systems remains a challenge. In this paper, we introduce ComPhy (CP), a novel modular framework designed to leverage the inherent physical structure of the problem to solve systems of PDEs. CP assigns each PDE to a dedicated learning module, each capable of incorporating state-of-the-art methodologies such as Physics-Informed Neural Networks or Neural Conservation Laws. Crucially, CP introduces an end-to-end alignment mechanism, explicitly designed around the physical interplay of shared variables, enabling knowledge transfer between modules, and promoting solutions that are the result of the collective effort of all modules. CP is the first approach specifically designed to tackle systems of PDEs, and our results show that it outperforms state-of-the-art approaches where a single model is trained on all PDEs at once.
